channel.name: Proprietary DRC deck violations with Calibre – Impact on Chip Functionality and Reliability

messages.content:
Hi everyone,

We found several violations in proprietary GF180MCU DRC deck used with Calibre, while KLayout DRC checks passed with 0 violations.
I have limited physical design and signoff experience, so I would appreciate the community's advice on whether these violations could affect chip functionality or manufacturability.

I/O library: gf180mcu_fd_io

**DRC Results**
*Counts: Template GDS → Precheck GDS.*

- DCF.5 (0 → 44,808): Requires ≥1.5 µm spacing between dummy COMP and Poly2. 
-- In our design: All markers involve 5 × 5 µm dummy COMP enclosed by 5.6 × 5.6 µm Poly2 fill. Precheck remaps Poly2 `30/4 → 30/0`.
We found a related PR #40 in precheck, but I'm still unsure whether these violations can be ignored.
- PAD.17 (176 → 176): Requires ≥15 µm between pad opening and COMP. 
-- In our design: Violations originate from PDK I/O cells (3.485 µm) and seal ring (12 µm).
- PAD.18 (98 → 163): Requires ≥15 µm between pad opening and Poly2. 
-- In our design: Violations involve PDK I/O Poly2 (12.855 µm) and dummy Poly2 fill (6.9–10.1 µm). Additional markers appear after precheck remapping.
- PAD.19a_M1 (60 → 60): Requires ≥6 µm between pad opening and non-pad Metal1. 
-- In our design: All markers involve existing PDK I/O geometry (3.540–5.665 µm).
- PAD.19a_M2 (10 → 28): Requires ≥6 µm between pad opening and non-pad Metal2. 
-- In our design: Violations involve PDK I/O geometry (5.665–5.950 µm) and dummy Metal2 fill (5.4 µm).
- G_HVNESD.10 (4 → 4): Recommends 1.5 µm spacing between well-tap and active COMP. 
-- In our design: All results originate from unmodified PDK I/O cells (2.0 µm).

Questions:
1. Could these violations affect chip functionality or manufacturability? Are they acceptable for tapeout?
2. Are violations from existing PDK geometry and precheck fill conversion known and acceptable?
3. Is WEDGE bonding with CUP disabled correct for wafer.space's default CoB packaging?

Any insights or recommendations would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you very much!

1. If it's in the foundry cells the chip won't be broken because it tripped a DRC rule in your commercial DRC engine.
2. Sounds like the open PDK contains geometry that's not particularly functional electrically where Calibre gets angry about it which would be appropriate if the structures would be electrically active.
3. Technically yes, if you order default COB, but almost all the PAD rules are just advisory/bond-house-originated. The seal ring seems to not hit the special treatment for your DRC engine.

`PAD.19a_M2` is also basically just about CUP.
Dummy metal should be harmless from how I understand the risks of CUP-despite-wedge-bonding, and foundry cells are essentially immune _anyways._

I am wondering if some of those could be contributing factors to the difficulty in bonding the chips and maybe the IO cells from GF are only suitable for ball bonding and not wedge bonding 🤔  ( cc @Tim 'mithro' Ansell / @stuart  )
Thank you for the detailed explanation!
BTW The Calibre deck is proprietary not commercial.
The IO's are described as `gf180mcu_fd_io 5V Inline non-CUP GPIO` in the PDK - https://gf180mcu-pdk.readthedocs.io/en/latest/IPs/IO/gf180mcu_fd_io/index.html

@Edmund - Please make sure you are running the wafer.space precheck on https://platform.wafer.space, because no matter what Calibre says, if you fail the wafer.space precheck you won't make it on the shuttle.

messages.content: Yes, we will make sure that! Thanks for reminding me.
@Edmund Are you running the non-CUP rules (the calibre rule deck has an option) with the non-CUP gpio (there are different libraries for CUP cells and non-CUP cells)?
Yes. I checked both sides: the layout uses GF’s gf180mcu_fd_io non-CUP GPIO library, and the Calibre run log shows bond_type WEDGE, with CUP_CHK disabled.
https://gf180mcu-pdk.readthedocs.io/en/latest/physical_verification/design_manual/drm_09_2.html, here also show that PAD.17, PAD.18, PAD.19a are checked by "Wedge type Wire bond (without CUP)"
Changed the channel name: Proprietary DRC deck violations with Calibre – Impact on Chip Functionality and Reliability

We ran the calibre rule deck on the non-CUP gpio library for the chipathon 2026 chips and only got `PAD.16` (due to missing guard ring) and `G_HVNESD.10` (in the `in_c` and `bi_24t` cells.

Is there a flat/hierarchical option?
Yes, we used hierarchical option (calibre -drc -hier)
I’m also curious whether PAD.18 ran with zero results in your report or was listed as "not executed".
Someone else actually ran the job and just gave me the error files.
@bailey I can see PAD19 violation just by looking at the cell.
What's the cell name?
I was looking at `in_c` but pretty sure it's all of them because it's in the guard ring that's common to all of them
I guess it can depend on the definition of "Circuit Metal1" and "Active Circuit COMP".  If that doesn't include guard rings and metal tying those guard rings then it's fine.

But then again, just because the naming of the IO library in the PDK says "non-CUP" doesn't mean it's actually suitable for wedge bonding either ...   wedge bonding implies non-CUP but non-CUP doesn't mean wedge bonding ...  So it's conceivable to me that the  IO library was designed for ball bonding and doesn't use CUP because even with ball bonding, although CUP is _possible_ it's still a pain and requires more care ....
Possibly; but I'd assume they target low-cost bonding with that just like they target low cost chips with gf180mcuD; and pretty sure Al wedge is substantially cheaper than Gold ball at scale.
Also I'd expect the sheer pad opening as such to not be too important for the practical effects of PAD.19, but rather that the pad bond target spot to the non-pad underlying metal is what matters?

Err ... (1) they probably have other io library fo gf180mcu ... just not ones they released or have the rights to do so.
(2) AFAIU wedge bonding is harder on the chip, more energy transfered so metal getting squished and moves a bit wouldn't surprise me.  We see pads shorted to GND ... those come from _somewhere_ ...
.....there's a line of GND just outside the pad....
(on all metal layers, notably)
Is there ? The scribe line isn't actually wired to gnd.

if realistic it might be useful to do bond testing prior to glob-topping and to set some samples that have this fault aside so some can meet an electron microscope to look at the surface structure around the failed bond?

<https://gf180mcu-pdk.readthedocs.io/en/latest/physical_verification/design_manual/drm_12_2.html>
This is a substrate tap.
The closed GND line is that metal1 line violating PAD.19
A short to substrate tap wouldn't show as such a low resistance to GND.
(sorry initially attached image of flip chip mode seal ring; important aspect wasn't changed though)

why?
Are you sure the massive amounts of substrate taps in the rest of the die will be that high resistance through the substrate to the _entire seal ring?_
It's a _massive_ 16um wide by the entire chip circumference substrate tap.
Heh, I have my doubt. But even then. This is > 12 um away while you have a m1 gnd line a mere 3 um away ...
But that 12 um is another guideline violation since recommentation is 30 um.
<https://gf180mcu-pdk.readthedocs.io/en/latest/physical_verification/design_manual/drm_09_2.html> ..... we're not meeting `PAD.15`....
I measure 12.
and only 11u gap between the metal of the ring and the metal of the pad.
FWIW These I/O cells might predate these rules and GF just kind of "grandfathered" them in or something?

A while back I was trying to understand if the proprietary DRC deck had name matching violation ignore type things in them (which probably wouldn't match the open source names for the cells) but I'm not sure I found before getting distracted by other things.

Is there a chance we get some sample COBs with that GND-short issue possibly tested after the wedge bonding and prior to the encapsulation?
Just to have some samples of the issue; there was discussion from @tnt last year in https://discord.com/channels/836175121361666059/1438575045302554833 about getting some failure case sectioned/imaged to try and figure out how it's shorted to ground/how it might be fixed in the future?

A decent microscope image to see where the bond spot hit might already give insight; I'd not be surprised if it's some kind of alignment failure.

@namibj - That is a question for #📦-cob and probably @Lauri / @stuart ?

I think with the new bonding provider we are not regularly seeing anything like the GND-short issue we where previously?
if not a regular event then we could probably ignore that

@Tim 'mithro' Ansell I thought so but then in the samples I got, 3 out of 6 had issue. And most notably the gnd shorts were _not_ detected/reported as bad by the COB tester ... Not sure if that was fixed yet.
Stuart however made the comment that those stamples were made as a "rush order, get this done quickly" so maybe they weren't up to the standard of what they usually do.
Are you able to microscope see if any ground shorts might be too close to the guard ring?
(or otherwise not properly centered on the pad)
I tried. Don't have a microscope good enough to see anything.
(Although through the epoxy is not great)
Yeah.
@tnt / @Lauri - Any idea why the CoB tester didn't report the gnd shorts?

@tnt @Tim 'mithro' Ansell Tester does not have any knowledge about the die being tested. It doesn't know if the short is by deisgn or not. We need to add another layer on top that knows run number and die infromation to better determine if short is acceptable or not.

What I find more interesting though, is that 100% of shorts are on power pins. Any chance these are not wirebonding issue and instead are due to damaged capacitors?

@Lauri Well it knows if they are power pins, so that'd be a good start to validate those since on the default frame they should be power.

As for the short being on power pins only : Interesting thought.  On run #1 that was definitely not the case, we had short on data pins. Here I only observed on power but my sample size it's very small.  On one of the die I tried clearing the short by applying high amperage 6V. ( It's not entriely crazy, I actually cleared a short on a data pin on run #1 using that method and the die works fine now ).  That didn't work and what got hot was the die ( and now you can see a burnt bubble in the expoxy ... ).
I will check the other sample that I have that's shorted and see if it could be the caps on that one.
Is there a chance this is not a bond issue but a die yield aspect?
I think we can just say that a design which shorts other pins to GND is not wafer.space CoB bonding compatible?
@Lauri I checked on a sample I have that had power short to gnd and it's not the capacitor, I removed them and short is still present.

But your comment made me think too ... if it's not a bond issue, something else that all the power rails have in common is that they are exposed on the top metal so could be susceptible to die damage. Especially true for TT which runs a very dense PDN grid because we have hundreds of power domains with all the power switching per-project.
